paragraphs: The paper revisits how correlation measures relationships that consistently increase or decrease, even when those relationships are curved. Pearson’s correlation is commonly treated as a measure of linear dependence. The authors investigate whether changing its mathematical normalization can extend what it captures while retaining its connection to covariance.

Their starting point is that Pearson’s correlation scales covariance using a bound supplied by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. They show that the choice of scaling bound affects the range of relationships a coefficient can capture, with tighter bounds expanding that range. They derive a tighter inequality and use it to construct a measure called rearrangement correlation.

The resulting coefficient captures arbitrary monotone relationships, including nonlinear ones, and reduces to Pearson’s correlation in linear scenarios. Simulations and real-world investigations report more accurate measurement of nonlinear monotone dependence than the classical and newer measures considered. The contribution is a principled adjustment to covariance normalization, with both a mathematical account of its scope and empirical evidence for its usefulness.
neurips-2024-adjust-pearson-s-r-to-measu.tldr: Rearrangement correlation adjusts Pearson’s covariance normalization to capture nonlinear as well as linear monotone relationships.

paragraphs: This paper approaches language-model alignment as a problem of controlling the model’s internal state during generation. Fine-tuning can demand substantial computing resources and suffer from unstable training. Existing techniques that operate at test time, such as prompting and guided decoding, also remain dependent on the original model’s capabilities. The authors investigate representation editing as another way to pursue specific objectives.

They describe an autoregressive language model as a stochastic dynamical system that evolves in discrete steps. External control signals intervene in its hidden representations. To choose those signals, the method trains a value function directly on hidden states using the Bellman equation, connecting internal states to the objective the controller seeks to achieve.

At test time, gradient-based optimization uses this value function to find control signals. Experiments report better performance than existing test-time alignment techniques and substantially lower resource requirements than fine-tuning approaches. These findings support using learned evaluations of internal states to guide generation, with the alignment intervention expressed directly through the model’s representations.
neurips-2024-aligning-large-language-mod.tldr: The method aligns language models by learning a value function that guides edits to hidden states during generation.

paragraphs: ALPS addresses the cost of storing and running large language models by improving one-shot pruning: removing weights without retraining the model. At language-model scale, existing approaches often use heuristics because solving the pruning optimization problem is expensive. The paper develops an optimization-based approach intended to make that more systematic treatment practical.

The framework uses operator splitting to tackle the pruning problem, followed by a post-processing step based on preconditioned conjugate gradients. It combines techniques for accelerating optimization and guaranteeing convergence with vectorization and GPU parallelism. These components connect the mathematical pruning objective to an implementation designed for the scale of large models.

The authors report improvements in both the pruning objective and perplexity, especially at high sparsity. For LLaMA3-8B with 70% sparsity, ALPS reduces WikiText test perplexity by 29% and improves zero-shot benchmark performance by 8% relative to existing methods. Those results indicate that more effective pruning optimization can preserve substantially more model performance when a large fraction of weights is removed.
neurips-2024-alps-improved-optimization-.tldr: ALPS makes optimization-based one-shot pruning practical and reports stronger language-model performance at high sparsity.

paragraphs: The paper asks how little randomness an online decision-making algorithm can use while retaining the benefits of full randomization. It studies metrical task systems on metric spaces containing n points, where requests arrive over time. Performance is expressed through a competitive ratio, comparing an online algorithm’s cost with an optimal reference that knows the requests.

The main theorem converts any fully randomized algorithm into one using only 2 log n random bits, while worsening its competitive ratio by at most a factor of two. The randomness budget does not grow with the number of requests. This yields the first order-optimal barely random algorithms for this problem.

The authors also give an equivalent collective interpretation: multiple agents act as a team whose cost is their average individual cost. Their results imply an O(log² n) competitive guarantee once the team contains at least n² agents, compared with the stated Ω(n) single-agent bound. They discuss implications for distributed decision-making, advice complexity, and transaction costs, suggesting broader relevance for the relationship between limited randomness and coordinated action.
neurips-2024-barely-random-algorithms-an.tldr: Metrical task systems can retain nearly the same competitive performance using a randomness budget independent of the number of requests.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learner that encounters a sequence of linear bandit tasks sharing a low-dimensional representation. Each task has parameters in a common m-dimensional subspace of a larger d-dimensional space. Learning that shared structure can reduce repeated learning effort, but earlier theory typically assumes the tasks uniformly cover the shared subspace.

The authors remove this task-diversity assumption, which otherwise lets a learner uncover the representation before seeing every task. They develop an algorithm that learns and transfers the shared representation as tasks arrive. Their regret guarantee applies under an ellipsoid action-set assumption, so the theoretical result retains a specific condition on the choices available to the learner.

The bound can substantially improve on learning tasks without exploiting their common structure when there are sufficiently many tasks and m is much smaller than d. Synthetic-data experiments also show improvements over baseline algorithms that rely on task diversity. The contribution is a provable route to representation transfer without requiring the sequence of tasks to expose all shared directions uniformly.
neurips-2024-beyond-task-diversity-prova.tldr: The paper proves that sequential linear bandit tasks can benefit from shared representations without assuming task diversity.

paragraphs: This paper develops a quantum algorithm for linear-quadratic control, motivated by the growing computational burden of controlling large dynamical systems. As industrial models increase in dimension, conventional optimal-control methods incur substantial overhead. The authors address the complete control-learning procedure and establish a provable speedup over classical approaches.

Their algorithm follows a policy-gradient approach, improving a control policy through estimates of how its objective changes. A central component is a new quantum subroutine for solving the matrix Lyapunov equation. The authors incorporate this component into a quantum-assisted differentiable simulator that supports efficient estimation of the gradients needed for policy updates.

The abstract reports gradient estimation that is more accurate and robust than classical methods based on stochastic approximation, together with a super-quadratic speedup over the classical approaches considered. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first end-to-end application of quantum computing to linear control with provable quantum advantage. Its significance lies in connecting a quantum numerical subroutine to a complete optimization method for control.
neurips-2024-differentiable-quantum-comp.tldr: A quantum-assisted differentiable simulator enables a policy-gradient algorithm for linear-quadratic control with a provable super-quadratic speedup.

paragraphs: DiffGS tackles the generation of 3D Gaussian Splatting representations, which support fast, high-fidelity rendering. Generating these representations is difficult because they consist of discrete, unstructured collections of Gaussian primitives. The paper changes how this collection is represented so that a generative model can work with continuous functions.

The method separates the representation into three functions describing Gaussian probabilities, colors, and transforms. A latent diffusion model learns to generate these functions, either without conditioning or in response to supplied information. This separation gives the diffusion model a continuous representation of the properties needed to construct the final Gaussian collection.

A discretization procedure then extracts a chosen number of Gaussians through octree-guided sampling and optimization. This allows the generated functions to yield arbitrary numbers of primitives for rasterized rendering. The authors explore unconditional generation, conditioning on text, images, or partial Gaussian representations, and conversion from points to Gaussians. The central contribution is this functional representation and its connection to flexible generation and subsequent extraction of renderable primitives.
neurips-2024-diffgs-functional-gaussian-.tldr: DiffGS generates continuous Gaussian Splatting functions and converts them into flexible numbers of renderable 3D primitives.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to divide high-dimensional data into multiple interpretable representations. A useful representation should capture meaningful concepts, but separating those concepts often requires prior knowledge. The authors position their method between traditional linear approaches that struggle to model multiple spaces and more expressive deep models whose representations can be difficult to interpret.

Their method, supervised independent subspace principal component analysis, or sisPCA, extends PCA to learn several subspaces. It uses the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion to incorporate supervision while separating the subspaces from one another. The paper also establishes connections with autoencoders and regularized linear regression, relating its construction to familiar representation-learning and prediction methods.

Applications include breast cancer diagnosis using image features, aging-related DNA methylation, and single-cell analysis of malaria infection. These examples demonstrate the method’s ability to identify and separate hidden structures in data. In the malaria analysis, the authors identify distinct functional pathways associated with colonization. The findings illustrate how an interpretable decomposition can support analysis of meaningful biological variation.
neurips-2024-disentangling-interpretable.tldr: sisPCA extends PCA with supervision and subspace separation to uncover interpretable factors in high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Understanding a trained machine-learning model can require storing large collections of gradients or Hessian-vector products. These quantities support analysis of how training examples affect a model and how its loss behaves around its parameters. Their storage requirements become a major obstacle for modern models, and conventional sketching methods struggle under those constraints.

The paper introduces a framework for scalable sketching of both types of quantities, tailored to modern hardware. Sketching provides compact representations for these analyses, addressing the burden of retaining the original large objects. The authors accompany the framework with theoretical guarantees and demonstrate its use in several investigations of pretrained language models.

Those applications include training-data attribution, analysis of the Hessian spectrum, and computation of intrinsic dimension. Together, they connect the storage method to questions about training influence, loss geometry, and the dimensional structure of models. The authors report findings that challenge assumptions about language models’ intrinsic dimensionality and Hessian properties. The contribution therefore combines an analysis-enabling computational method with new observations obtained through its use.
neurips-2024-efficient-sketches-for-trai.tldr: Hardware-oriented gradient and Hessian-vector sketches make language-model attribution and loss-landscape analysis more scalable.

paragraphs: Temporal action segmentation identifies the stretches of a video associated with different actions. Strong results can require dense inputs, complicated models, and expensive post-processing. This paper seeks to reduce that computational burden by organizing prediction around complete segments and treating each video segment as an instance token within a Transformer.

The proposed network, BaFormer, combines two kinds of queries. Instance queries perform instance segmentation, while a global query predicts boundaries without assigning action classes to them. These predictions produce continuous segment proposals. At inference time, a voting procedure uses the instance-segmentation output to assign classes to the segments defined by those boundaries.

The resulting method operates in a single stage, combining boundary prediction and segment classification in an efficient pipeline. Across several popular benchmarks, the authors report better or comparable accuracy to DiffAct while using only 6% of its running time. This comparison supports the paper’s central proposal that segment-oriented prediction and boundary-aware voting can maintain strong segmentation quality with substantially less computation.
neurips-2024-efficient-temporal-action-s.tldr: BaFormer combines boundary prediction and query-based voting to segment video actions with substantially lower reported runtime.

paragraphs: This paper studies a platform that repeatedly posts a price to a buyer and seller whose valuations are private. A trade happens when both accept. Maximizing their combined utility can leave one participant with a very small share, so the authors instead reward the platform according to the smaller of the two participants’ utilities.

They first show that an algorithm with no regret for total utility can perform badly under this fairness objective. They then characterize what can be learned when feedback reveals only whether each participant accepted the price. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to the comparison used in the learning problem.

For T interactions, the regret is Θ(log T) in the deterministic setting. In the general stochastic setting, an Ω(T) lower bound rules out sublinear regret. When buyer and seller valuations are independent, the rate becomes Θ(T^(2/3)) up to logarithmic factors. The paper also gives tight bounds when valuations are fully observed. These results show how the fairness objective, feedback, and dependence between valuations jointly shape learnability.
neurips-2024-fair-online-bilateral-trade.tldr: Using the smaller trader utility as a fairness objective produces sharply different learning guarantees depending on feedback and valuation independence.

paragraphs: The paper introduces fast algorithms for integrating tensor fields on weighted trees. These operations combine information distributed across a tree, and straightforward computation can be expensive. The authors exploit structured-matrix theory, particularly low displacement rank, to obtain algorithms whose cost grows linearly with problem size apart from polylogarithmic factors.

They demonstrate applications in approximating graph metrics with tree metrics, classifying graphs, modeling meshes, and processing images with Topological Transformers. For the Transformer application, they introduce relative-position encoding masks that can require as few as three additional learned parameters per layer. These masks incorporate structural relationships into the model with a small parameter increase.

Most of the proposed integrators are exact: they are numerically equivalent to their brute-force counterparts. On graphs containing thousands of nodes, these exact algorithms deliver reported speedups of 5.7–13 times. The Transformer mechanisms produce reported accuracy gains of 1.0–1.5% or more. Alongside extensive theoretical analysis, these findings show how tree-based structure can support both faster numerical computation and useful model components.
neurips-2024-fast-tree-field-integrators.tldr: Structured-matrix methods accelerate tree-field integration, with mostly exact algorithms and applications extending to Topological Transformers.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for reusing simpler optimization algorithms on a broader family of objectives. It introduces upper-linearizable and upper-quadratizable functions, extending concavity and diminishing-returns submodularity across several settings. The treatment includes monotone and non-monotone objectives over different kinds of convex sets.

A general meta-algorithm converts methods for linear or quadratic maximization into methods for these broader function classes. The framework also supports conversions between feedback settings, including first-order information and zeroth-order observations, as well as semi-bandit and bandit feedback. This makes the approach useful when both the objective’s structure and the available information vary.

By using existing convex-optimization results as building blocks, the authors derive algorithms that improve prior results in several cases. They obtain the first dynamic and adaptive regret guarantees for the DR-submodular maximization settings considered, addressing performance as conditions change and over different portions of an online sequence. The paper reports these advances with fewer assumptions than previous results, making algorithm conversion the central source of its theoretical gains.
neurips-2024-from-linear-to-linearizable.tldr: A general conversion framework turns linear and quadratic optimization methods into algorithms for broader objectives and feedback settings.

paragraphs: Graph condensation creates a small graph intended to retain essential characteristics of a much larger graph dataset. This can make the data more manageable, but the growing number of proposed methods makes progress difficult to assess without comprehensive evaluation. GC-Bench addresses that need through a common benchmark and an accompanying software library.

The benchmark examines three dimensions: effectiveness, transferability, and complexity. This organizes evaluation around how well condensed graphs work, how their usefulness transfers, and the computational demands involved. The study compares 12 state-of-the-art condensation algorithms across 12 diverse graph datasets, covering both tasks about individual nodes and tasks about whole graphs.

The library supports training and evaluating different condensation methods, with reproducibility as an explicit goal. The contribution is a shared basis for systematic comparison across scenarios, alongside analysis of the evaluated methods’ behavior. Its scope makes graph condensation easier to study as a collection of performance and computational tradeoffs, rather than relying on isolated evaluations of individual algorithms.
neurips-2024-gc-bench-an-open-and-unifie.tldr: GC-Bench evaluates 12 graph condensation methods across 12 datasets and provides a library for reproducible comparisons.

paragraphs: Gradient-variation online learning seeks guarantees that reflect how much gradients change across a sequence of objectives. Existing analyses often assume a fixed global bound on how quickly gradients can vary with position. This paper studies a more flexible smoothness condition that allows smoothness to depend on gradient magnitude.

The authors extend optimistic mirror descent by examining stability along the optimization trajectory and using local smoothness information. They then design a single algorithm that obtains optimal gradient-variation regret guarantees for both convex and strongly convex functions without knowing the curvature in advance. This avoids having to select a separate method using prior curvature information.

The universal algorithm has two layers: a group of base learners and a meta-algorithm that combines them. A new Lipschitz-adaptive meta-algorithm handles potentially unbounded gradients while retaining the second-order bound needed for this combination. The paper applies the framework to fast convergence in games and stochastic extended adversarial optimization. Its contribution is to preserve variation-sensitive guarantees under a broader smoothness model.
neurips-2024-gradient-variation-online-l.tldr: The paper extends gradient-variation online learning to generalized smoothness and adapts to convexity without prior curvature knowledge.

paragraphs: Protein structure prediction benefits from multiple sequence alignments, which collect information about related proteins and their evolutionary variation. Predictions can suffer when too few related sequences are available to build a useful alignment. MSAGPT addresses this low-MSA setting by learning to generate alignments that provide informative input for structure prediction.

The model uses a two-dimensional evolutionary positional encoding to represent complex evolutionary patterns within alignments. It combines this with a flexible one-dimensional decoding framework that supports zero-shot and few-shot learning. The authors also show that feedback from AlphaFold2 can improve the model further through rejective fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from AlphaFold2 feedback.

Experiments report that MSAGPT generates faithful, informative alignments, with TM-Score improvements of up to 8.5% in few-shot scenarios. Transfer-learning results suggest potential for other tasks that depend on alignment quality. The contribution links generative modeling of evolutionary information to better inputs for downstream prediction, while demonstrating an additional route for improvement through feedback from a structure-prediction model.
neurips-2024-msagpt-neural-prompting-pro.tldr: MSAGPT generates informative protein sequence alignments to improve structure prediction when homologous sequence information is scarce.

paragraphs: Plan-on-Graph addresses how a language model searches a knowledge graph while answering a question. Knowledge graphs provide explicit, editable information that can help with outdated knowledge, hallucinations, and opaque reasoning. Existing approaches often fix the breadth of graph exploration manually and depend on navigating correctly without recovering from mistaken paths.

The proposed method first divides a question into several sub-objectives. It then repeatedly explores reasoning paths, updates its memory, and reflects on whether previous choices need correction. Exploration is adaptive to the question’s meaning, and the process continues toward an answer. This makes planning and revision recurring parts of graph-based reasoning.

Three mechanisms—Guidance, Memory, and Reflection—work together to support adaptive exploration breadth and self-correction. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and efficiency. The findings support a reasoning procedure that can use accumulated information to adjust its search and revisit errors. The contribution concerns the organization of knowledge-graph exploration, with explicit mechanisms for directing, retaining, and reassessing the reasoning process.
neurips-2024-plan-on-graph-self-correcti.tldr: Plan-on-Graph combines sub-objectives, memory, and reflection to adapt knowledge-graph exploration and correct mistaken reasoning paths.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether spatially selective place cells can emerge from learning to remember continuous sensory experiences. The authors model hippocampal area CA3 as a recurrent autoencoder that reconstructs experiences from noisy, partly hidden observations. Simulated agents follow rodent-inspired trajectories through arenas whose sensory properties vary smoothly across space.

Training combines accurate reconstruction and completion of partial experiences with a constraint on total activity. Under this setup, units in the encoding layer develop localized firing fields. The model reproduces several properties associated with hippocampal representations: remapping between environments, orthogonal spatial representations across arenas, multiple fields in larger or more complex spaces, and slow representational drift.

The authors argue that temporal continuity of experience during movement explains these outcomes. They predict that rapidly changing sensory context will disrupt place fields, and that blocking recurrence will prevent return to previously learned maps while still allowing fields to form. They also predict that the dimension of temporally smooth experience determines field dimensionality. These are testable predictions from the model, extending its proposed account beyond the simulated observations.
neurips-2024-time-makes-space-emergence-.tldr: Place-like fields emerge in an activity-constrained memory model trained to reconstruct temporally continuous sensory experiences.

paragraphs: Perceptual practice sometimes improves performance only under the trained conditions, while other training allows improvements to transfer. This paper proposes a dual-learning model to explain both patterns. Its central idea is that learning to perform a task and changing the sensory features used for that task operate on different timescales.

The fast process adapts task performance using feature representations that already exist. The slower process changes those representations to match shifts in environmental statistics. According to the model, repeatedly presenting the same stimulus condition triggers feature learning and produces specificity. When stimulus conditions vary during training, task learning dominates and produces transfer.

The interaction also explains a transition from transfer to specificity as training under a single condition accumulates. The authors show that the model can account for both effects observed in classical psychophysical experiments. This offers a unified interpretation of apparently conflicting learning outcomes through differences in training conditions and duration. The broader proposal is that perceptual learning balances adapting to a task with the effort of modifying representations.
neurips-2024-to-learn-or-not-to-learn-th.tldr: A model combining fast task learning and slow feature learning explains both transfer and specificity in perceptual practice.

paragraphs: TopoFR investigates how face-recognition models can preserve structural information already present in large training datasets. The authors observe that directly aligning structure between input data and learned representations leads to overfitting and collapse of structure in the latent space. Their method addresses both how structure is aligned and which training examples receive attention.

The first component, PTSA, uses persistent homology to align the topological structures of the input and latent spaces. This provides a way to preserve structural information while improving generalization. The second component, SDE, computes a structure damage score for each sample, identifies difficult examples, and directs the model to prioritize their optimization.

Together, the components connect a global concern—maintaining useful structure in the representation—with attention to individual samples that damage that structure. Experiments on popular face-recognition benchmarks report stronger performance than the state-of-the-art methods considered. The findings support topology alignment and structure-aware hard-sample mining as complementary tools for improving the learned space used in face recognition.
neurips-2024-topofr-a-closer-look-at-top.tldr: TopoFR improves face recognition by aligning topological structure and prioritizing samples that damage the learned representation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces time-series editing: modifying an existing sequence according to requested attributes while aiming to preserve its other properties. Relevant attributes include trends, seasonality, and external information such as location. This adds a form of targeted manipulation beyond the unconditional and conditional synthesis approaches described in the paper, which generate sequences from scratch.

The authors identify two challenges: limited coverage in the available data and complex relationships between sequences and their attributes. They propose a diffusion model called TEdit to address them. A bootstrap learning algorithm expands the effective coverage of the original data, supporting learning beyond the combinations directly represented in the initial dataset.

TEdit also uses modeling and generation at multiple resolutions to capture relationships between time-series patterns and attributes. Experiments demonstrate its effectiveness at editing specified attributes of existing sequences. The contribution includes both the definition of an editing task and a model designed around its requirements, bringing attribute-directed changes to data where preserving the surrounding temporal properties is part of the objective.
neurips-2024-towards-editing-time-series.tldr: TEdit uses diffusion, bootstrap learning, and multiple resolutions to edit specified attributes of existing time series.

paragraphs: Analog in-memory computing offers a promising route toward more energy-efficient AI, but training on non-ideal analog devices creates optimization problems. This paper develops theory for gradient-based training in that setting. It focuses on why stochastic gradient descent can retain an error even after training has continued for a long time.

The authors identify asymmetric device updates as the cause of this failure to converge exactly. They derive a lower bound on the asymptotic error, establishing that the residual error reflects a fundamental limit of SGD-based analog training in the studied setting. It therefore cannot be dismissed as looseness in the analysis.

The paper then studies Tiki-Taka, a heuristic analog-training algorithm previously observed to outperform SGD empirically. The authors prove that it can converge exactly to a critical point and eliminate the asymptotic error identified in their analysis. Simulations support the theoretical results. Exact convergence here concerns reaching a critical point; the stated finding does not identify that point as a global optimum.
neurips-2024-towards-exact-gradient-base.tldr: The paper explains SGD’s residual error on asymmetric analog devices and proves exact critical-point convergence for Tiki-Taka.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning depends on augmentations that create different views of graph data. Existing augmentation techniques can be tied to particular scenarios, expensive to select or generate, and restricted to a finite set of available transformations. This paper seeks a common mechanism that can accommodate varied graphs and tasks.

The authors reinterpret augmentation through message passing and introduce a unified graph augmentation module, UGA. They show theoretically that it can unify explicit augmentations involving nodes, edges, attributes, and subgraphs. This shifts the design from separately handling those transformation categories to expressing them through a shared module.

They build a framework called GOUDA around UGA, combining commonly used contrastive losses with an independence loss. The combination addresses the need for augmented views to retain consistency while also providing diversity. Evaluations across multiple datasets and tasks demonstrate generality and efficiency relative to existing state-of-the-art graph contrastive methods. The contribution combines a theoretical unification of augmentations with a learning framework that uses that flexibility across different scenarios.
neurips-2024-unified-graph-augmentations.tldr: GOUDA uses a unified message-passing view of graph augmentation to support consistent, diverse views across graph-learning scenarios.

paragraphs: A weighted graph’s metric backbone retains the edges belonging to shortest paths and removes edges for which a shorter route exists between their endpoints. This creates an apparent problem for community structure. Dense communities offer many alternative internal routes, while edges between communities often serve as bridges, so pruning appears likely to weaken the distinction between communities.

Earlier empirical work nevertheless found that metric backbones preserve community structure well in real networks. This paper investigates that discrepancy mathematically. The authors analyze a broad class of weighted random graphs with communities and prove that their community structure is robust to removing every edge outside the metric backbone.

They also compare graph sparsification techniques empirically, finding support for the theoretical result and showing that the metric backbone is an efficient sparsifier when communities are present. The result explains why preferentially deleting many within-community edges need not destroy the larger grouping structure. Its formal guarantee concerns the analyzed random-graph class, while the empirical comparison provides complementary evidence about the sparsification method.
neurips-2024-why-the-metric-backbone-pre.tldr: The paper proves community robustness under metric-backbone pruning for a broad weighted random-graph class and supports it empirically.

paragraphs: WindsorML is an open dataset intended to support development and testing of machine-learning surrogate models for external automotive aerodynamics. It contains 355 geometric variants of the Windsor body. The variants exhibit a range of flow characteristics representative of those observed around road cars, providing varied examples for learning relationships between geometry and aerodynamic behavior.

Each example comes from a GPU-native, wall-modeled large-eddy simulation using a Cartesian immersed-boundary method. The simulations use more than 280 million cells to pursue high fidelity. The paper discusses validation of the underlying computational fluid dynamics methods, connecting the released data to an assessment of the simulation approach that produced it.

The dataset includes geometry, three-dimensional time-averaged volume and boundary data, and force and moment coefficients. These outputs support studying both distributed flow behavior and aggregate aerodynamic quantities. The authors describe the release as, to their knowledge, the first large-scale, high-fidelity Windsor-body CFD dataset under a CC-BY-SA license. Its principal contribution is a substantial shared resource for building and evaluating aerodynamic surrogate models.
neurips-2024-windsorml-high-fidelity-com.tldr: WindsorML provides high-fidelity aerodynamic simulations for 355 Windsor-body geometries to support machine-learning surrogate models.
